places.name: Mossdale Crossing
places.text: The freeway crosses the San Joaquin River here, near a steel railroad lift bridge. The first railroad bridge at this spot opened on September 6, 1869, and that afternoon the first through train from Sacramento crossed it, reaching Alameda by evening, where a ferry waited for San Francisco. It was the last link of the first transcontinental railroad to the Pacific.
places.more: Long before the railroad, a sharp bend slowed the river here and made a shallow ford, a favorite fishing ground of the Yokuts, whose homeland this is. The Spanish called it El Pescadero, the fishing place. In 1848 John Doak and Jacob Bonsell started the first ferry across the San Joaquin here, pulling a barge along a rope stretched from shore to shore. They charged a dollar for a person on foot and eight dollars for a wagon and horses. William Moss, a former Ohio riverboat captain, bought the ferry in 1856, and the valley beside it became Moss' Dale. By August 1869 about 600 men were building the railroad bridge, 500 of them Chinese. A reporter wrote that the last rail went down at 3 in the afternoon, just before the first train crossed. The wooden swing bridge was rebuilt in steel in 1895 and replaced with today's lift bridge in 1942.
places.spot: Look for the steel railroad lift bridge crossing the river near the freeway.

places.name: Manteca, a dairy town named lard
places.text: Highway 120 leads east to Manteca, whose name is Spanish for lard. That is an odd name for a town whose railroad stop was there to ship dairy products, and nobody agrees on how it happened. One story says locals wanted a word for butter and the railroad got it wrong. The authors of a county history think the Southern Pacific simply liked giving its stops appealing Spanish names.
places.more: Joshua Cowell, the town's founder, brought dairy farming to the area. The railroad stop was first called Cowell Station, but the line had a second Cowell Station, named for his brother Henry, so a new name was needed. A local legend says residents chose the name Monteca and the railroad misprinted it, but a local columnist points out that the word monteca is nowhere to be found in Spanish dictionaries. When Manteca incorporated in 1918, Cowell was elected its first mayor. As recently as the 1970s Manteca lived mostly on farming. Rising Bay Area home prices then turned it into a commuter town, and its population has more than tripled since 1980.

places.name: Lathrop, born of a quarrel
places.text: Lathrop exists because of a quarrel. When Stockton dragged its feet on where the railroad should run, Central Pacific president Leland Stanford built the line around the city and started a new town here, at a depot called Wilson's Station. In 1869 it was renamed for the family of his wife, Jane Lathrop Stanford, and her brother Charles, an engineer for the railroad.
places.more: By 1871 Lathrop was an important division point and rail stop, and the railroad built a $50,000 hotel here, said to be one of the largest in California at the time. About 600 people lived here by 1879. In the 1880s the railroad moved its roundhouse and machine shop to Tracy, and Lathrop began a decline that lasted nearly 50 years, with a major fire in 1911 along the way. World War Two brought Permanente Metals, which made aircraft parts and magnesium bombs, and the Sharpe Army Depot, one of the Army's major supply depots in the West. Lathrop did not become a city until 1989. Today large planned neighborhoods, among them River Islands, spread west of the freeway.

places.name: Flying Scotsman in hiding
places.text: The Roth Road exit is signed for Sharpe Depot, an Army supply base. In 1972 it became a hiding place for Flying Scotsman, often called the world's most famous steam locomotive. Its owner had gone bankrupt touring it across North America, so he stored the engine at the Army depot here, out of reach of his creditors.
places.more: Built in 1923, Flying Scotsman was the first steam locomotive officially clocked at 100 miles per hour, and it retired from regular service in 1963 after running more than 2 million miles. Businessman Alan Pegler bought it and, with support from the British government, sent it touring the United States and Canada from 1969 to promote British exports, fitted with a cowcatcher, a bell and an American-style whistle. The tour ran 15,400 miles, but some states treated the steam engine as a fire hazard, and in 1972 Pegler, deep in debt, declared bankruptcy. After the engine sat at Sharpe Depot, businessman William McAlpine paid the debts and bought it for $72,000. It sailed home through the Panama Canal, landed at Liverpool in February 1973 and steamed to Derby along a route lined with crowds.

places.name: French Camp
places.text: French Camp is considered the oldest settlement in San Joaquin County. From about 1832 to 1845, French Canadian trappers working for the Hudson's Bay Company camped here every year with their families. It was the southernmost regular camp of fur brigades sent all the way from Fort Vancouver, in what is now Vancouver, Washington. The place was also called Castoria, from castor, the Latin word for beaver.
places.more: Its Spanish name, Campo de los Franceses, the field of the Frenchmen, lived on in a Mexican land grant of 1844. That year Charles Weber and William Gulnac promoted the first colony of white settlers on the grant, which took in both French Camp and the future site of Stockton. The camp sat at the southern tip of the southernmost slough of the Delta, so boats could reach it, and a trail led from here into the Sierra foothills. That trail later became an alternate route for the Mariposa Road, favored in the rainy season because it drained so well, and it survives as French Camp Road. Today French Camp is home to the county hospital and an Army depot.

places.name: First Sikh temple in America
places.text: About a mile east of the freeway, on South Grant Street, is the first Sikh house of worship in the United States. Gurdwara Sahib Stockton opened on October 24, 1912, in a house. Its founders were Punjabi Sikh immigrants who farmed the land around Stockton.
places.more: One founder, Jawala Singh, was a successful potato farmer who worked a 500-acre ranch next to Stockton with his partner Wasakha Singh. Sikh farmers newly arrived from Punjab first gathered to pray in a room on that ranch. Jawala Singh went on to help form the Ghadar Party, a movement that called for an end to British rule in India. The Stockton gurdwara backed it, sponsoring the first Punjabi-language newspaper in the United States. The gurdwara also paid for the university studies of Dalip Singh Saund, who later became the first Sikh American and the first Asian American elected to Congress.

places.name: Little Manila
places.text: Highway 4 heads east from here on the Crosstown Freeway, built in the early 1970s through part of Little Manila. By 1946 this downtown neighborhood, south of Main Street, held the largest Filipino community in the United States. Residents fought the freeway and lost, and it displaced many Filipino homes and businesses.
places.more: Many young Filipino men came to Stockton for farm work. Racist laws kept most of them from marrying, and they were even barred from crossing Main Street into what was then the white north side of town. So they built their own community, with hotels, barber shops, restaurants and social clubs. Labor leaders such as Larry Itliong, Carlos Bulosan and Philip Vera Cruz all worked out of Stockton, and Filipino farmworkers and leaders like them were behind the success of the United Farm Workers. The community raised money to build the Filipino Plaza, completed in 1972, which became home to displaced families and to the Barrio Fiesta, a Filipino cultural festival held each August. The Little Manila Foundation works to save the last remaining buildings.

places.name: Stockton, once Tuleburg
places.text: When Charles Weber laid out a town here in 1849, he called it Tuleburg. He soon renamed it for Commodore Robert Stockton, a famed naval commander of the Mexican-American War. That made Stockton the first town in California with a name that was neither Spanish nor Native American. As the head of navigation on the San Joaquin River, it boomed as a supply stop for gold miners.
places.more: This is the homeland of the Yatchicumne, a branch of the Northern Valley Yokuts, who built their villages on low mounds to stay above the regular floods. One village, Pasasimas, stood on a mound beside what is now the Stockton Channel downtown. Weber, a German immigrant, got the land as part of a Mexican land grant. In its early years Stockton also went by Weberville, Fat City and Mudville, and it is one of a handful of cities that claim to have inspired the 1888 poem Casey at the Bat. Thousands of Chinese immigrants arrived in the 1850s, and by 1880 Stockton had the third-largest Chinese community in California.

places.name: Port of Stockton
places.text: The docks just west of the freeway belong to the Port of Stockton, a seaport more than 70 nautical miles from the ocean. Ocean ships up to 900 feet long come up a dredged channel, 35 feet deep, from San Francisco Bay. The modern port opened on February 2, 1933, when the ship Daisy Grey arrived with a load of lumber from Oregon.
places.more: Stockton and Sacramento are the only inland seaports in California. During the Gold Rush the San Joaquin River was deep enough for ocean-going vessels, which made Stockton a natural supply point for miners. The first freight vessel, the sloop Maria, called here in 1848. During World War Two the War Department wanted ships built at an inland port, safe from attack on the coast, so many new ships were built here. The Navy's supply depot on Rough and Ready Island, a major communications post for submarines in the Pacific during the Cold War, is now the port's West Complex. By land area it is the second largest port in California, covering about 4,200 acres.
places.spot: Look for big warehouses and docks beside the ship channel, and maybe an ocean freighter.

places.name: University of the Pacific
places.text: About a mile and a half east of the freeway is the University of the Pacific. It was the first university chartered in California, in 1851, and it started out in Santa Clara. It moved to San Jose in 1871 and to Stockton in 1924.
places.more: Pacific also opened the first medical school on the West Coast, in 1858. That school later became the Stanford University School of Medicine. Its Conservatory of Music, founded in 1878, was the first of its kind west of the Mississippi, and the pianist and composer Dave Brubeck graduated from Pacific in 1942. Because the brick buildings, tower and rose gardens look like an old East Coast college, Hollywood has filmed here many times, including scenes for Raiders of the Lost Ark. The Calaveras River flows through the campus.

places.name: Calaveras River, river of skulls
places.text: The freeway crosses the Calaveras River here. Calaveras is Spanish for skulls. The river is said to have been named in 1806 by the Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga, when he found many skulls of Native people along its banks.
places.more: Moraga believed the people had died of famine or in fights over hunting and fishing grounds. Another story says an 1836 party that included John Marsh and José Noriega camped along the river one evening and woke to find skulls and bones all around them, and they gave it the same name. The Calaveras runs about 52 miles from Calaveras County to the San Joaquin River, with just one reservoir along the way, New Hogan Lake. It and its side channel, Mormon Slough, wrap around central Stockton, so much of the city is really one of the many islands of the Delta.

places.name: Benjamin Holt and the Caterpillar
places.text: The Benjamin Holt Drive exit shares its name with a Stockton inventor. On Thanksgiving Day, November 24, 1904, Holt tested a tractor that rode on tracks instead of wheels, plowing soggy Delta farmland near Stockton. A company photographer was reported to have said it crawled like a caterpillar. Holt liked it: Caterpillar it is, he said, and the name lives on in the company Caterpillar Inc.
places.more: Holt came to Stockton in 1883 and, with his brothers, started a company that made wagon wheels, then combine harvesters and tractors. Most of the fields around Stockton had been reclaimed from the Delta, and tracks spread a heavy machine's weight so it would not sink into the soft ground. During World War One, Allied armies used about 10,000 Holt vehicles, many of them hauling heavy guns. Holt died in 1920, and five years later his company merged with its biggest rival, the C. L. Best company, to form what is now Caterpillar Inc. A restored Holt Caterpillar tractor from around 1918 is on display at the Haggin Museum in Stockton.

places.name: The last piece of I-5
places.text: A 4.6-mile stretch of freeway north of Stockton was the very last piece of Interstate 5 to open. On October 12, 1979, after 26 years of construction, the consuls of Canada and Mexico joined California's transportation secretary to cut a gold-colored chain, completing Interstate 5 from the Mexican border to the Canadian border.
places.more: California's transportation secretary, Adriana Gianturco, compared the moment to the driving of the golden spike on the transcontinental railroad. The West Side Freeway, the stretch of I-5 down the west side of the San Joaquin Valley, was built in three phases starting in the early 1960s. Once the second phase opened in 1972, traffic picked up, because in Stockton the new freeway came within 4 miles of the Golden State Highway, Route 99. The third phase, finished in 1979, carried I-5 north to Sacramento and joined it to the northern half of the freeway.

places.name: Lodi, wine and root beer
places.text: Highway 12 leads east to Lodi, a town surrounded by vineyards. Its growers raise more than 130 grape varieties, and many of the old vines here were planted between the Gold Rush and Prohibition. Lodi is also the birthplace of A&W Root Beer: in 1919 Roy Allen sold his first batch from a cart during a parade, and a plaque marks the spot.
places.more: The town was first called Mokelumne, after the nearby river, but that caused confusion with other towns, so the name was changed. Nobody is sure why Lodi was chosen. One story credits a record-setting local trotting horse, another the Italian town where Napoleon won his first victory, but most likely some early settlers came from a place called Lodi in Illinois. From the early 1900s into the 1980s, Lodi promoted itself as the Tokay Capital of the World, for the Flame Tokay grapes grown here. Every September the town holds the Lodi Grape Festival. The Creedence Clearwater Revival song Lodi is named for this town, although songwriter John Fogerty admits he had never been here and simply thought it was the coolest sounding name.

places.name: Delta asparagus
places.text: From about 1900 through the 1970s, asparagus was a signature crop of the Delta west of here. The first commercial crop was grown in 1892 on Bouldin Island by Chinese farmers. Every spear was cut by hand, with a long knife slipped just below the surface of the sticky peat soil, and crews walked each field every few days during the spring harvest.
places.more: Chinese immigrants did the first hand labor, followed by Japanese workers, then Filipinos, and later Mexican workers. In 1930 the Delta had more than 350 asparagus camps holding about 7,000 harvest workers, 5,500 of them Filipino. In 1919 Thomas Foon Chew, known as the Asparagus King, moved his Bayside Cannery to Isleton, on the Sacramento River, and at its peak it was the third-largest canning company in the country. Later, railroad ice cars let growers ship spears fresh instead of canned, and plantings grew again. By the mid-1980s, competition from lower-wage countries such as Peru and Mexico had shrunk the crop, and fresh Delta asparagus has become hard to find.

places.name: Sandhill crane reserve
places.text: A couple of miles west of the freeway, off Woodbridge Road, is the 353-acre Woodbridge Ecological Reserve, also called the Isenberg Sandhill Crane Reserve. Sandhill cranes arrive in the Delta around late September and spend the fall and winter here. Sunset is the best time to watch them fly in, giving a loud, trumpeting call that can be heard from a long way off.
places.more: Sandhill cranes have one of the longest fossil histories of any living bird, and the oldest sure fossil is 2.5 million years old. Their wings spread about six and a half feet. In winter, unrelated cranes band together in groups that feed and roost together. The reserve's south site is open to the public at any time of day or evening. The north site, with its crane viewing shelter, can be visited only on docent-led tours, held on weekends from October through February. California listed the greater sandhill crane as threatened in 1983, after its numbers fell. Each November, Lodi holds a Sandhill Crane Festival.

places.name: The Delta, California's Holland
places.text: West of the freeway lies the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, about 57 reclaimed islands and tracts ringed by 1,100 miles of levees. Once the marsh was drained, its peat soil met the air and slowly broke down, and the land has sunk as much as 25 feet since the late 1800s. Much of the western and central Delta now sits at least 15 feet below sea level.
places.more: Over thousands of years, tules and reeds grew and decayed here into peat as much as 50 feet deep, which is why the soil is so rich. The Delta is the homeland of Miwok and Maidu people, whose villages of 200 to 1,000 people stood along its eastern edge, where the land was higher and less likely to flood. They built houses, boats and clothing from tules. Chinese laborers did much of the first levee building, from the 1850s to the 1870s. About half of all the river water in California flows through the Delta, and water pumped from its southern end helps supply some 23 million people. Since 1900 the levees have failed more than 160 times, and in 2004 a single break flooded all of Jones Tract.

places.name: Mokelumne, People of the Fish Net
places.text: The freeway crosses the Mokelumne River here, about half a mile below the spot where the Cosumnes River flows into it. Both names come from Miwok. Mokelumne joins moke, a fishnet, with umne, people of, so it means People of the Fish Net. Cosumnes is thought to be built the same way, from kosum, salmon.
places.more: This lower river country is thought to be mostly Plains Miwok homeland, with many villages once standing between the Sierra foothills and the edge of the Delta. The Miwok called the river Wakalumitch, possibly meaning big river. A Spanish missionary first wrote the name down as Muquelumnes in 1817, and John C. Frémont is credited with today's spelling. Far upstream, Pardee Dam, finished in 1929, feeds the Mokelumne Aqueduct, which carries the river's water across the Delta to the East Bay. The aqueduct is the only water supply for about 1.4 million people there. Downstream from here, the Mokelumne splits in two around Staten Island before it reaches the San Joaquin.

places.name: Locke, a Chinese river town
places.text: About three miles west of the freeway, on the Sacramento River levee a mile north of Walnut Grove, is Locke, the last of the Sacramento River Chinatowns to be built. Immigrants from Heungshan County, in Guangdong, built it up after a 1915 fire destroyed the Chinese community in Walnut Grove. California's Alien Land Law barred them from owning land, so they leased about nine acres from George Locke and owned only their buildings.
places.more: Three Chinese merchants put up the first buildings here in 1912. The fire of October 7, 1915, burned both the Chinatown and the Japantown of Walnut Grove. At times as many as 1,000 to 1,500 Chinese people lived in Locke, with the numbers swelling during the growing and harvest seasons. For decades the residents could not buy the land under their homes. A developer bought the town from the Locke heirs in 1977, Sacramento's housing and redevelopment agency bought it in 2002, and in 2004 the agency finally let longtime residents buy their land. Locke became a National Historic Landmark in 1990.

places.name: Cosumnes River Preserve
places.text: The Cosumnes River Preserve, whose visitor center is just east of the freeway, covers nearly 50,000 acres, including some of the largest remaining wetlands and streamside habitat in the Central Valley. The Cosumnes is one of very few rivers on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada without a major dam, so it still floods over its banks in season, creating important habitat for wintering birds.
places.more: The visitor center is on Franklin Boulevard, and the preserve is managed by a partnership of state, local, federal and private groups. Raptors, herons, sandhill cranes, shorebirds and waterfowl all use it. The river still floods hard: its most notable floods of recent decades came in 1986, 1997, 2017 and 2023. The 1997 storm was the largest on record and broke through many of the Cosumnes levees. Proposals to dam the main river have largely stalled, partly because of its free-flowing status and its value for wildlife.

places.name: Stone Lakes National Wildlife Refuge
places.text: The freeway runs along the eastern edge of Stone Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, set aside in 1994. It holds seasonal and permanent wetlands, grasslands, streamside forest and some of the last remaining freshwater lakes in the Central Valley. It lies in the Delta, the destination of thousands of migrating waterfowl, shorebirds and other water birds.
places.more: The refuge protects wild habitat and farmland in an area squeezed by urban growth, between the city of Elk Grove and farm country. It holds a major rookery where great blue herons and other birds nest together in colonies. Threatened and special-status species here include the valley elderberry longhorn beetle, the Swainson's hawk and the greater sandhill crane. The refuge has a mile of paved trail loops around managed wetlands and a natural playscape for children, but no visitor center. Volunteers with the Friends of Stone Lakes teach visitors about this refuge on the edge of the city.
places.spot: Look for marshes and ponds near the freeway, and maybe a tall great blue heron.

places.name: Elk Grove
places.text: Elk Grove Boulevard leads east into Elk Grove, which began in 1850 as a stagecoach stop for travelers between Sacramento and the Bay Area, when James Hall opened the Elk Grove Hotel. Hall is said to have named it for elk antlers he found in the groves nearby, though he had also lived in a Missouri town with the same name.
places.more: When the Central Pacific's tracks came through in 1868, about a mile east of the original town, a second Elk Grove Hotel went up near the railroad. Elk Grove stayed a small farm town for more than a century, until suburbs began spreading here in the late 1980s, and it did not become a city until July 1, 2000. In 2004 and 2005 it was declared the fastest growing city in the country, and its population nearly tripled between 2000 and 2020. Elk Grove is also the home base of the Wilton Rancheria, a federally recognized tribe of Miwok people. The federal government ended the tribe's recognition in 1958, and the tribe won it back in 2009. In 2022 it opened Sky River Casino in Elk Grove, on the site of a half-built shopping mall.

places.name: Freeport, a town born of taxes
places.text: The tiny river town of Freeport, just west of the freeway, began as a way around Sacramento's port taxes. In 1862, businessmen tired of paying taxes at Sacramento's riverfront landing formed the Freeport Railroad Company to build a new port, free of those taxes, with a railroad that bypassed Sacramento. The town boomed for three years and reached 300 to 400 people.
places.more: The plan was for the Freeport Railroad to meet the Sacramento Valley Railroad halfway between Sacramento and Folsom, so freight could skip Sacramento entirely. The boom did not last. Freeport sits on the east bank of the Sacramento River about 7.5 miles south of downtown, and the 2020 census counted just 58 people here. Its drawbridge across the river, a bascule bridge, opened in 1929 and was rebuilt in 1955.

places.name: Sacramento Zoo and Land Park
places.text: The Sutterville Road exit leads to William Land Park and the Sacramento Zoo, a few blocks east of the freeway. The zoo opened on June 2, 1927, as the William Land Park Zoo, with 40 animals gathered from local parks, among them monkeys, raccoons, birds and deer.
places.more: In 1948 the Sacramento Union newspaper ran a fund drive to buy the zoo an elephant, and in 1949 she arrived. Two local sisters named her Sue, for Sacramento Union Elephant. The zoo grew from 4.2 acres to 14.3 acres in the early 1960s and had just over 500 animals by 2012. A 2024 plan to move it to a bigger site in Elk Grove was cancelled in April 2025 over cost, and the city council approved an expansion where it is. The park around it is named for William Land, a pioneer who built the Western Hotel in 1875. It also holds Fairytale Town, a park whose play equipment is based on fairy tales and nursery rhymes, and Funderland, with small carnival rides for young children.

places.name: The Boat Section
places.text: Through downtown Sacramento, I-5 runs below the water table, close beside the Sacramento River. Caltrans calls this stretch the Boat Section. It was built below street level in the 1960s and 1970s so the freeway would stay out of view of downtown offices and shops, and pumps, drains and a retaining wall keep the river's seepage out.
places.more: To build it, crews dug out the site and pumped away the water that seeped in, and in 1980 record rains flooded it with 15 feet of water. Sacramento has fought water from the start. In the Great Flood of 1862 the American River put much of the city under water for three months, and the newly elected governor, Leland Stanford, had to go to his own inauguration by rowboat. So from 1862 until the mid-1870s the city raised its downtown, building brick walls along the streets and filling them with dirt, and old first floors became basements. Parts of this Sacramento Underground can still be seen. Between the freeway and the river lies Old Sacramento, a 28-acre historic district with 53 historic buildings.
places.spot: Look for the walls of this sunken stretch of freeway, built below street level.

places.name: Tower Bridge
places.text: The gold towers just west of the freeway belong to the Tower Bridge, a lift bridge over the Sacramento River dedicated in 1935. Its 160-foot towers hold counterweights as heavy as the 1,150-ton middle span, so just two 100-horsepower electric motors can raise it to let tall boats through.
places.more: It replaced a 1911 railroad bridge, and trains crossed it until 1962. Its smooth, sheathed towers are a rare use of Streamline Moderne styling on a lift bridge. At the dedication on December 15, 1935, a thousand homing pigeons were released to carry the news across California. For years the bridge was painted silver, and in 1976 it was painted yellow ochre to match the gold-leafed cupola of the nearby State Capitol. In 2001, residents living within 35 miles voted on a new color scheme, and all gold beat two other choices. Just upriver, the Delta King, a 285-foot sternwheel steamboat that ran to San Francisco from 1927 to 1940, is tied up as a hotel. Across the river, the minor-league ballpark Sutter Health Park became the temporary home of the Athletics in 2025.
places.spot: Look for the two tall gold towers of the Tower Bridge.

places.name: California State Railroad Museum
places.text: The California State Railroad Museum, in Old Sacramento, holds 21 restored locomotives and railroad cars, some dating back to 1862. Inside, a large mock-up recreates railroad construction high in the Sierra at Donner Pass around 1867. It features the Central Pacific's first locomotive, the Gov. Stanford, which came to California in pieces by ship, around Cape Horn.
places.more: Nearby, at the foot of K Street, the Central Pacific, the western half of the first transcontinental railroad, broke ground on January 8, 1863. Its president, Leland Stanford, was governor of California at the same time. Chinese laborers did most of the heavy work of carrying the line over the Sierra Nevada, and in 1869 it met the Union Pacific at Promontory Summit. East of the freeway, the railroad's shops grew into the biggest railroad facility west of the Mississippi, employing about a third of Sacramento's workers in the early 1900s. The railroad's lawyer, Edwin Crocker, brother of partner Charles Crocker, spent his railroad fortune on art, and his family's gallery became the Crocker Art Museum, the oldest art museum in the western United States. The museum's collection includes the only surviving Southern Pacific cab-forward, a 1944 steam locomotive with the engineer's cab at the front.

places.name: Where two rivers meet
places.text: The freeway crosses the American River here, close to where it flows into the Sacramento. The park at the meeting of the two rivers, Discovery Park, is designed to flood. In winter high water it can end up underwater, taking pressure off the American River levees.
places.more: Maidu, Miwok, Nisenan and Wintun peoples have lived along the American River for at least 5,000 years, and the Nisenan call it Kum Sayo, roundhouse river. A Spanish expedition under Gabriel Moraga named it the Rio de las Llagas, the River of Wounds, perhaps because of hostile encounters with Native people. On August 13, 1839, John Sutter arrived at the meeting of the rivers, and the next year his party built Sutter's Fort. In 1848 gold was found upstream at Sutter's Mill, starting the Gold Rush. Today the American River is the main source of drinking water for Sacramento.

places.name: ARCO Arena, gone but loud
places.text: Just east of the Arena Boulevard exit stood ARCO Arena, home of the Sacramento Kings from 1988 to 2016. Built for just 40 million dollars, it was the cheapest arena in the NBA and the smallest. In 2013 it set a Guinness World Record for the loudest sports roar, at 126 decibels.
places.more: When it opened, the arena sat in an isolated spot on the growing northern edge of the city. It hosted concerts, ice shows, rodeos and monster truck rallies, and at one time nearly two million people a year came through its doors. LeBron James played his first regular-season NBA game here on October 29, 2003, scoring 25 points in a loss to the Kings. The Kings moved to the new Golden 1 Center downtown in 2016. The site was donated in 2021 to California Northstate University for a medical school and hospital, and after a free farewell event in March 2022, the arena was torn down later that year.

places.name: Airport and the big red rabbit
places.text: Sacramento International Airport, just north of the freeway, opened on October 21, 1967, with a single 8,600-foot runway. Inside Terminal B is one of its odder sights: Leap, a 56-foot red rabbit by the artist Lawrence Argent, made to look as if it had jumped into the building from outside. It weighs about 10,000 pounds.
places.more: The airport opened as Sacramento Metropolitan Airport with five airlines: Pacific Air Lines, Pacific Southwest Airlines, United, Western and West Coast Airlines. It took over from the old municipal airport, now Sacramento Executive Airport. Today it covers about 6,000 acres, which is said to make it the largest commercial airport in California by land area. The new Terminal B opened on October 6, 2011. The rabbit is made of aluminum, steel, granite and bronze, and the airport leaves the question of why a red rabbit unanswered, so visitors can make up their own story.

places.name: Crossing the Sacramento River
places.text: The freeway crosses the Sacramento River here, the line between Sacramento and Yolo counties, on the Elkhorn Bridge, built in 1969 and also called the Vietnam Servicemen Memorial Bridge. The Sacramento is the largest river in California. It flows about 400 miles from the Klamath Mountains to the Delta and drains some 26,500 square miles.
places.more: In 1808 the Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga named it the Rio del Santisimo Sacramento, the river of the Most Holy Sacrament. A writer with the expedition is quoted describing oaks and cottonwoods hung with grapevines, chattering birds and big fish in the clear water, and the Spaniards exclaiming that it was like the Blessed Sacrament. By flow it is the second-largest river on the Pacific coast of the lower 48 states, after the Columbia, and it supplies more than 80 percent of the fresh water that reaches the Delta. Its watershed had one of the densest Native populations in California, and it once carried one of the southernmost big runs of Chinook salmon in North America.

places.name: Yolo Bypass
places.text: The Elkhorn Causeway here crosses the Yolo Bypass, a floodway 41 miles long and about 3 miles wide. When the Sacramento River runs high, it spills over weirs into the bypass, which can carry about four times the river's own flow and turns into an inland sea. That takes pressure off the levees and lowers the flood risk for Sacramento and Davis.
places.more: The two main weirs are the Sacramento Weir, built in 1916, whose 48 gates are opened by hand with long hooked poles, and the two-mile-long Fremont Weir, finished in 1929, which simply overflows when the river gets high enough. Cache Creek drains in from the west as well. In late spring and summer much of the bypass is farmed, mostly in rice, along with safflower, tomatoes, corn and sunflowers. The floods make a rich nursery: young Chinook salmon grow much faster in the bypass than in the river itself. The bypass also holds the Vic Fazio Yolo Wildlife Area, a haven for waterfowl, shorebirds and wading birds.
places.spot: Look for the wide, flat floodway beside the causeway, flooded in wet years and farmed in summer.

places.name: Knights Landing
places.text: County Road 102 leads north to Knights Landing, on the Sacramento River. Dr. William Knight, a physician from Baltimore, founded it in 1843 on a mound that had long been a meeting place for the Native people living around Cache Creek and the river. It grew into a steamboat landing and a ferry crossing.
places.more: When the town was laid out in 1849 it was named Baltimore, but a dispute over selling the town lots cost it that name. This is Patwin homeland, and a Patwin group called the Yolotoi lived near Woodland and close to present-day Knights Landing. On March 25, 1890, the Southern Pacific finished a branch line to the town, and a bridge across the river later added greatly to its prosperity. Its cemetery is one of several places said to hold the unmarked grave of the stagecoach robber Black Bart. About 1,100 people live there today.

places.name: Woodland, City of Trees
places.text: Woodland is the county seat of Yolo County and calls itself the City of Trees, for the valley oaks planted around town. In 1853 Henry Wyckoff built a store here called Yolo City. Frank Freeman bought it in 1857, gave land to anyone who would clear it and build a home, and in 1859 suggested the name Woodland.
places.more: Woodland took over as county seat in 1862, after a flood hit the old seat at Washington, now part of West Sacramento. For decades it grew on farming, with three rice mills, a sugar beet refinery and a tomato cannery, and in the 1950s it was said to have the most millionaires per capita of any city in California. Downtown, the Woodland Opera House, first built in 1885 and rebuilt after a fire in the 1890s, was the first opera house to serve the Sacramento Valley, and John Philip Sousa and his band played there. It closed in 1913 and stayed dark for decades. Now a state historic park, it puts on shows again. Woodland's 1905 library is the oldest Carnegie-funded library still operating in California.

places.name: Woodland tomato cannery
places.text: The big plant half a mile from the freeway is the Woodland tomato cannery. Tomatoes have been processed and canned here since 1958, under owners including Contadina and Del Monte, and Pacific Coast Producers has run it since 2001. It works in season, generally July through September, and handles about 495,000 tons of tomatoes a year.
places.more: That is close to a billion pounds of tomatoes in about three months. Washing the fresh tomatoes takes a lot of water, and recycled water from the plant's cooling towers makes up about 30 percent of each day's wash water. Mud that comes in from the fields with the tomatoes settles out in tanks. The wastewater is then sprinkled over about 900 acres of fields roughly four miles southeast of the plant, planted mostly in grasses such as Bermuda grass, which soak up nitrogen.

places.name: Capay Valley, Yocha Dehe homeland
places.text: Highway 16 heads west past Esparto into the Capay Valley, which Cache Creek flows through. The valley is the traditional home of Patwin, or southern Wintun, people, and today it is home to the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, a federally recognized Patwin tribe. The tribe is headquartered in Brooks, in the valley, where it runs the Cache Creek Casino Resort.
places.more: The Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation was formerly known as the Rumsey Indian Rancheria of Wintun Indians, and its Rumsey Rancheria, established in 1907, covers 185 acres. Traditional Patwin life included fishing for king salmon, harvesting acorns, hunting and gathering. Spanish missionaries enslaved many Patwin, and epidemics of malaria in the early 1830s and smallpox in 1837 killed many of the survivors. Today the tribe also farms, growing wine grapes and olives and selling olive oil, vinegar and wine under its Seka Hills brand. In the 1800s the valley belonged to a Mexican land grant, Rancho Canada de Capay.

places.name: Cache Creek, the trappers' creek
places.text: The freeway crosses Cache Creek here. Its name comes from Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers, who cached, or hid, their furs along the Sacramento River and its smaller streams. They called this one Riviere la Cache. One of their camps, which early settlers knew as French Camp, stood in an oak grove on the creek's north bank, about a mile east of the town of Yolo.
places.more: Cache Creek runs 87 miles from the outlet of Clear Lake, through a canyon and the Capay Valley, then out across the valley floor. A diversion dam built near Capay in 1914 sends its water through about 175 miles of canals across Yolo County. Near its end the creek spreads into a settling basin east of Woodland, whose overflow reaches the Yolo Bypass in floods. The creek was a trade route long before the trappers came: the main trading trail of the Patwin followed it. In 1906 the San Francisco earthquake set off a landslide that briefly dammed the creek upstream, north of Rumsey.

places.name: Yolo, place of rushes
places.text: The little town of Yolo shares its name with the county, and the name comes from the Patwin language. Nobody is quite sure of its source. It may come from Yo-loy, said to mean a place abounding in rushes, from a village called Yodoi near Knights Landing, or from that village's chief, Yodo. In the state's original 1850 law, the county was spelled Yola.
places.more: Before it settled on Yolo, the town went by Cacheville, Cochran's Crossing, Hutton's Ranch and Travelers Home. About 425 people lived here at the 2020 census. Yolo County was one of California's original counties, created at statehood in 1850. Its rural roads are mostly numbered rather than named, with each whole-number road generally a mile from the next, which is why exits here are signed for roads like County Road 102 and Road 22.

places.name: Sunflower seed fields
places.text: Some fields in this part of the valley grow sunflowers for planting seed, not for snacks. California has historically produced about 95 percent of the hybrid sunflower seed planted in the United States, and a quarter of the world's supply, with seed fields in Yolo County and elsewhere in the Sacramento Valley. Bees carry pollen between interplanted rows of male and female plants to make the hybrid seed.
places.more: Hybrid seed grows into plants with more vigor and other traits farmers want. But the business has been shrinking here. Certified hybrid sunflower seed fields in California topped 53,600 acres in 2018 and fell to about 27,000 acres by 2023, as seed companies moved production overseas. Pioneer said it no longer needed the extra production capacity at its Woodland location, because it had enough capacity in Europe for the European market, and one grower blamed the exchange rate for pulling production back to Europe.

places.name: Zamora, cut by the highways
places.text: The farm community of Zamora was once called Black's, after J. J. Black, who settled here in 1865. When the Northern Railway built its line north from Woodland in the 1870s, Black donated a strip of land for a depot, and a little town grew up around the station, with a hotel, stores, a jail, blacksmith shops and six warehouses.
places.more: As one local history puts it, modern highways rolled through in 1949 and 1969, cutting the heart from the town. What remained was a town with no services: a rebuilt IOOF hall, a rebuilt town hall, a planing mill, St. Agnes Catholic Church, the school building and a few houses. County officials estimated just 61 residents in 2005. This is Patwin homeland. Patwin hunters stalked deer, tule elk and antelope here and hunted ducks, geese and swans with bows and nets in the tule marshes. As of 1994, dozens of families had farmed or lived in the Zamora district for three generations or more.

places.name: Sutter Buttes on the horizon
places.text: On a clear day, a jagged cluster of peaks rises out of the flat valley far to the north. These are the Sutter Buttes, the worn remains of a volcano that was active roughly a million and a half years ago. They form a rough circle about 10 miles across and are often called the world's smallest mountain range.
places.more: The highest point, South Butte, rises a little over 2,100 feet. The Maidu name, Histum Yani, the Nisenan name, Estom Yanim, and the Wintun name, Onolai-Tol, all roughly mean the Middle Mountains. In Maidu and Nisenan religion, the Buttes are the place where dying people go to ascend to the afterlife. Almost all of the land around them is privately owned by ranchers and farmers, so hiking there is limited to trips led by a few local groups, such as the Middle Mountain Foundation.
places.spot: Look for a jagged clump of mountains standing alone on the flat valley floor.

places.name: I-505, once I-5W
places.text: Interstate 505 meets I-5 here and runs south to I-80 at Vacaville. It was first planned as part of I-5W, a western loop of Interstate 5 through the Bay Area, while the route through Sacramento was to be I-5E. The split numbering was dropped, and the western loop became parts of I-580, I-80 and I-505.
places.more: The northernmost piece of I-505, from Highway 16 at Madison to this junction, opened in August 1977. Today it is the main route between the Bay Area and the northern Sacramento Valley, letting drivers skip Sacramento and its traffic. It is a four-lane freeway its whole length and skirts the eastern edge of the city of Winters. Most other split Interstates around the country were renumbered too, but I-35E and I-35W survive in Texas and Minnesota.

places.name: Dunnigan, once Antelope
places.text: Dunnigan began as Antelope. In the winter of 1853, a flood washed two settlers, Copp and Wilson, off their claims near the Sacramento River, and they moved up to higher ground here. The following year a Yolo County postal worker named A. W. Dunnigan arrived and went into the hotel business with Henry Yarick. Their inn was known simply as Dunnigan's, and the town took his name.
places.more: A post office opened here in 1856, and the first store in 1866. The railroad arrived in 1876, the same year the post office changed its name from Antelope to Dunnigan. This is Patwin homeland. Today Dunnigan is a small freeway community of about 1,400 people, nearly 40 miles from both Vacaville and Sacramento.

zones.label: San Joaquin River and Lathrop
zones.text: The freeway crosses the San Joaquin River at Mossdale and runs through Lathrop, a railroad town where large planned neighborhoods now spread west of the freeway.

seasons.winter: On some winter days, tule fog blankets this part of the valley.

zones.label: Stockton
zones.text: I-5 runs through Stockton, past the deepwater port and its channel to San Francisco Bay, and crosses the Calaveras River.

seasons.winter: Nearly all of Stockton's rain falls from October through April, and tule fog blankets the city on some winter days.
seasons.summer: Summers here are very hot and dry.

zones.label: Lodi vineyards and the Delta's edge
zones.text: Vineyards spread east toward Lodi, while the flat, reclaimed islands of the Delta, held in by levees, stretch off to the west.

seasons.fall: Sandhill cranes arrive around late September and spend the fall and winter in the fields and wetlands west of the freeway.
seasons.winter: Cranes, geese and swans use the Woodbridge reserve as their winter home.

zones.label: Cosumnes wetlands and Elk Grove
zones.text: Wetlands of the Cosumnes River Preserve lie near the freeway, which runs along the eastern edge of the Stone Lakes refuge as it passes through Elk Grove.

seasons.winter: Seasonal floods on the undammed Cosumnes River create important habitat for wintering birds.

zones.label: Along the river to Land Park
zones.text: The freeway runs close to the Sacramento River through the south side of Sacramento, near William Land Park and the zoo.

zones.label: Downtown Sacramento
zones.text: I-5 runs in a sunken trench between downtown and the river, past Old Sacramento and the Tower Bridge, and crosses the American River near where it meets the Sacramento.

seasons.winter: In winter high water, Discovery Park, where the two rivers meet, can end up underwater, as it is designed to.

zones.label: The airport and the Sacramento River
zones.text: North of downtown the freeway passes the old ARCO Arena site and the airport and crosses the Sacramento River, the line between Sacramento and Yolo counties.

zones.label: Yolo Bypass
zones.text: The long Elkhorn Causeway crosses the Yolo Bypass, a floodway that becomes an inland sea in big floods and is farmed, mostly in rice, the rest of the time.

seasons.winter: In wet winters and springs, the bypass floods and becomes a huge wetland for birds and young salmon.
seasons.summer: In late spring and summer, much of the bypass is farmed in rice, safflower, tomatoes, corn and sunflowers.

zones.label: Woodland and Cache Creek
zones.text: The freeway passes Woodland, a farm town with a big tomato cannery, and crosses Cache Creek beside the little town of Yolo.

seasons.summer: From July through September, the Woodland tomato cannery works through about 495,000 tons of tomatoes.

zones.label: Zamora and the Dunnigan Hills
zones.text: Farm country continues past Zamora and Dunnigan, near the Dunnigan Hills, and on clear days the Sutter Buttes rise from the valley floor to the north.

trivia.q: Manteca, the name of a dairy town, is Spanish for what?
trivia.why: Manteca means lard, an odd name for a town whose railroad stop shipped dairy products.

trivia.q: Which famous British steam locomotive was hidden from creditors at an Army depot in Lathrop in 1972?
trivia.why: Its bankrupt owner stored Flying Scotsman at Sharpe Depot until a new owner paid the debts and shipped it home.

trivia.q: French Camp's other old name, Castoria, comes from the Latin word for which animal?
trivia.why: Castor is Latin for beaver, a nod to the camp's role in the fur trade.

trivia.q: The Calaveras River has a Spanish name. What does calaveras mean?
trivia.why: Calaveras means skulls; the river is said to be named for skulls a Spanish expedition found on its banks in 1806.

trivia.q: Benjamin Holt's 1904 track-type tractor gave its name to which company?
trivia.why: A company photographer reportedly said the machine crawled like a caterpillar, and Holt adopted the name.

trivia.q: In what year did the final stretch of I-5 open, just north of Stockton?
trivia.why: The last 4.6 miles opened on October 12, 1979, completing the freeway from Mexico to Canada.

trivia.q: Which drink was first sold in Lodi in 1919?
trivia.why: Roy Allen sold his first batch of A&W Root Beer from a cart during a parade in Lodi.

trivia.q: About how many miles of levees ring the Delta's islands?
trivia.why: About 1,100 miles of levees protect the Delta's islands, many of which sit below sea level.

trivia.q: In Plains Miwok, Mokelumne means people of the what?
trivia.why: Moke means fishnet and umne means people of.

trivia.q: How was the Tower Bridge's gold color chosen?
choices: By a vote of local residents
trivia.why: In 2001 residents living within 35 miles voted, and all gold beat two other color schemes.

trivia.q: What giant animal sculpture is inside Terminal B at Sacramento's airport?
trivia.why: Leap, a 56-foot red rabbit by the artist Lawrence Argent, is in Terminal B.

trivia.q: Cache Creek is named for what?
choices: Furs that trappers hid along it
trivia.why: Hudson's Bay Company trappers cached their furs along the Sacramento River and its streams.
